chapters.title: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
chapters.overview: An introductory chapter on how science works at the secondary stage: using simplified models, precise scientific language, symbols, units and mathematics, and the meaning of laws, theories and principles. It stresses prediction, the openness of science to correction by evidence, rough estimation as a scientific skill, and the connections between physics, chemistry, biology, earth science and other disciplines.

sections.title: Example 1.1: A cricket shot
points: Science uses models: simplified ways of looking at real systems that keep only what matters for a given question.
Examples: a moving car as a point, atoms as spheres and bonds, cells as labelled diagrams, the Earth as a layered sphere.
Building models involves deliberate assumptions, e.g. neglecting air resistance for a falling object.
For a six in cricket, the mass, speed and direction of the ball matter; bat brand or ball colour do not, and spin or seam have small effects that can be ignored.
Meghnad Saha treated star matter as a hot gas and focused on temperature, pressure and ionisation to link star colour to temperature.

sections.title: Airplane fuel miscalculation
points: Everyday words like force, work, cell or reaction have specific, precise meanings in science.
Quantities are represented by symbols (m, v, F, I) each with a defined unit.
Mathematics is a language: an equation is a compact statement of how quantities are related, not just a calculation tool.
An aircraft ran out of fuel because the ground crew used fuel density in pounds per litre instead of kilograms per litre; using SI units everywhere avoids such errors.
Standard units are based on international standards, ensuring fairness in trade; the speed of light c comes from the Latin celeritas and is exactly 299792458 m/s.

sections.title: Example 1.2: How do we check predictions?
points: A law describes a regular pattern in nature; a theory explains why patterns occur based on evidence; principles are broad ideas applied to situations.
A theory is not a guess; scientific ideas are open to improvement as new evidence appears.
Well-established laws, theories and models allow predictions, which are reasoned expectations based on evidence.
A prediction like 'it will rain because clouds look dark' becomes testable by asking about measurable data and past patterns (humidity, wind, temperature).
Weather forecasts go wrong because tiny differences in conditions grow over time; theories may fail under new conditions, and scientists then re-examine assumptions using evidence.

sections.title: Checking ‘viral’ claims on social media: Is eating food harmful during an eclipse?
points: Claims can be disproved by asking simple scientific questions.
An eclipse is a play of shadows; no physical, chemical or biological mechanism makes food harmful during it.

sections.title: Example 1.3
points: A useful habit: understand the situation, identify the quantities that matter, then make a rough estimate to check if an answer makes sense.
Estimating rice needed for a family of four for a month uses daily calorie needs of about 2000–2500 kcal per adult.
Breathing about 12–15 breaths a minute over 1440 minutes gives about 20 thousand breaths; at about 0.5 litre per breath this is about 10,000 litres of air a day.
A cross-check using balloons (3 balloons a minute of 2 litres) gives about 8640 litres, reasonably close to the first estimate.

sections.title: How does a mask really work?
points: Science is divided into physics, chemistry, biology and earth science only to organise knowledge; nature has no such boundaries.
Real problems like climate change, medicines or sustainable technology need several disciplines together.
Understanding a mask needs physics (particle motion, electrostatic attraction), chemistry (polymer fibres), biology (viruses) and mathematics (modelling airflow and filtration).
Science is a human activity shaped by curiosity, creativity, collaboration and careful questioning, developed across cultures and generations.

keyTerms.meaning: A simplified way of looking at a real system that focuses only on what is most important for a given question.
Usually describes a regular pattern observed in nature, often expressed using words or mathematical relationships.
An explanation of why patterns occur, based on evidence gathered over time; not a guess or untested idea.
A broad idea that helps us make sense of a given situation, e.g. conservation of energy when climbing stairs.
A reasoned expectation, based on evidence and careful thinking, of what will happen under new or different conditions.
An approximate value used to check whether a result is reasonable or impossible.

keyResults.label: Speed of light
keyResults.statement: Denoted c (from Latin celeritas); defined to be exactly 299792458 m/s.

keyResults.label: Limit of forecasts
keyResults.statement: Weather forecasts are usually reliable for a few hours or days but less certain further ahead, because tiny differences in conditions grow over time.

keyResults.label: Estimate: air breathed per day
keyResults.statement: About 20 thousand breaths of about 0.5 litre each, roughly 10,000 litres of air a day.

chapters.title: Cell: The Building Block of Life
chapters.overview: The chapter introduces the cell as the basic structural and functional unit of life, starting with how microscopes let us study cells and estimate their size. It describes the cell membrane (osmosis, fluid-mosaic model), the cell wall, prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and the organelles of eukaryotic cells. It then explains cell division by mitosis and meiosis, the Cell Theory, and why cells have a definite life span, with cancer as loss of growth control.

sections.title: How to Study Cells?
points: The limit of resolution of the human eye is 0.1 mm: two points closer than this, viewed from about 25 cm, appear as one.
Cells are usually too small to see unaided, so convex lenses (objective and eyepiece) are used to magnify them.
Robert Hooke first observed cells in 1665 in a thin slice of cork using a self-designed microscope of about 200–300X.
Cell size can be estimated by dividing the diameter of the field of view (in µm) by the number of cells across it; total magnification is eyepiece power times objective power.
Microscopes were improved in resolution, contrast and magnification; electron microscopes use a beam of electrons to show cell structure at the nanometre scale.

sections.title: Structure of a Cell
points: Cells interact with one another and their surroundings at the cell boundary, where substances move in and out.
Even single-celled organisms exchange materials and respond to their environment through the cell membrane.

subsections.title: Cell membrane — The universal feature of a cell
points: The cell membrane (plasma membrane) is a thin boundary that protects the cell's contents and is selectively permeable.
A potato piece swells in plain water and shrinks in 20 per cent salt or sugar solution because water, but not solute, crosses the membrane.
Diffusion is net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration; osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
Solutions are isotonic, hypotonic or hypertonic depending on outside solute concentration compared with inside the cell.
The membrane is 7 to 10 nm thick, made of lipids and proteins; the fluid-mosaic model describes a lipid bilayer with embedded proteins whose molecules can move.

subsections.title: Cell wall — The outer covering of cells
points: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside the membrane to withstand wind and rain and keep leaves and plants firm and upright.
The cell wall is permeable, letting water and dissolved minerals through.
In concentrated sugar solution plant cells lose water but keep their shape; the membrane pulls away from the wall, while cheek cells shrink.
The plant cell wall is mainly cellulose; fungi and bacteria also have cell walls, and animal cells have none, which makes them flexible.

sections.title: The Cell Interior — A Coordinated Working System
points: Most cells have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus; the cytoplasm contains organelles, mostly visible only with an electron microscope.
Prokaryotic cells (e.g. bacteria) lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells (plant and animal) have both.
Prokaryotic cells are typically 1 to 10 µm and usually unicellular; eukaryotic cells are 10 to 100 µm and can be unicellular or multicellular.
The cytoskeleton, a network of fine fibres, gives support, shape, movement and internal transport; stored starch or crystals are cell inclusions.

subsections.title: Why do eukaryotic cells need these organelles?
points: Organelles carry out different life processes independently at the same time, like parts of a tiny living factory.

subsections.title: Nucleus — House of coded instructions
points: The nucleus has a double-layered nuclear membrane with pores; the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits.
Chromosomes, made of DNA and proteins, carry hereditary information; functional segments of DNA are genes.
In a non-dividing cell DNA is part of chromatin, which organises into chromosomes before division.
Mature human RBCs lack a nucleus and live about 120 days; in prokaryotes the DNA region is the nucleoid.

subsections.title: Ribosomes — The protein factories
points: Ribosomes lie free in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER and are the sites of protein synthesis.

subsections.title: Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) — Manufacturing factory
points: The ER is a network continuous with the nuclear envelope, involved in synthesis and transport of proteins, lipids and some hormones.
Rough ER has ribosomes and makes and secretes proteins; smooth ER lacks ribosomes and makes and stores fats and hormones.

subsections.title: Golgi apparatus — The packaging and shipping centres
points: Stacks of flattened sacs that act as the cell's post office, modifying, sorting and packaging proteins and lipids into vesicles.
First observed in 1898 by Camillo Golgi in nerve cells of a barn owl and confirmed later by electron microscopy.

subsections.title: Lysosomes — The clean-up system
points: Single membrane-bound sacs of enzymes that break down unwanted molecules and damaged cell parts; products are reused.
Lysosomal enzymes in sperm help break down the outer layer of the egg during fertilisation.

subsections.title: Mitochondria — The powerhouse of the cell
points: Each mitochondrion has a smooth porous outer membrane and an inner membrane folded into cristae.
Glucose is broken down in cellular respiration and the energy is stored as ATP, the energy currency.

subsections.title: Plastids — Centre for food synthesis in the plant cells and beyond
points: Chloroplasts are double-membrane plastids with stroma and chlorophyll-containing discs that absorb light for photosynthesis.
Mitochondria and plastids have their own DNA and ribosomes, suggesting a shared evolutionary history with bacteria.
Chromoplasts hold yellow, orange or red pigments that colour flowers and fruits; leucoplasts are colourless and store starch, oils or proteins.

subsections.title: Vacuoles — The organelles for storage and support
points: A mature plant cell has a large central vacuole filled with cell sap, storing water, minerals, sugars and waste.
The vacuole keeps the cell firm; when it loses water the plant wilts. Animal cells have small, temporary vacuoles.

sections.title: How do Normal Cells Grow and Divide?
points: Cells grow only to a certain size; body growth and healing happen because cells divide to replace old or damaged cells.
Onion root tip cells show different stages of cell division because they divide continuously.
Hundreds of billions of cells, almost 1 per cent of body cells, are replaced daily; eukaryotic cells divide in an orderly cell cycle.

subsections.title: Cell division
points: Cell division forms new cells from pre-existing cells for growth, repair and reproduction.
The two major types are mitosis and meiosis.

subsections.title: Mitosis
points: The most common division; produces two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent.
Important for growth, repair, maintenance and asexual reproduction.

subsections.title: Meiosis
points: Produces gametes only in reproductive organs (testes, ovaries, anthers, plant ovaries) and creates variation.
The parent cell divides twice to form four daughter cells with half the chromosome number; fertilisation restores the number.
Errors in mitosis can cause tumours; errors in meiosis can cause genetic disorders, pregnancy loss or reduced fertility.
Cell culture grows cells outside the body in a nutrient-rich sterile medium for research and producing medicines and vaccines.

sections.title: Cell Theory — The Unifying Principle of Biology
points: Schleiden (1838) showed plants are made of cells, Schwann (1839) showed animals are, and Virchow (1855) added that new cells come only from pre-existing cells.
The classical Cell Theory unifies biology and explains life's continuity through cell division.

subsections.title: Do cells grow and reproduce forever?
points: Every cell has a definite life span and is replaced when it dies.
Many animal cells stop dividing on contact with neighbours (contact inhibition); cancer cells lose this and form tumours.
Plant cells, with rigid walls, do not show contact inhibition.
Programmed Cell Death removes cells selectively, e.g. between developing fingers; Haberlandt (1902) proposed plant cell totipotency.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Questions ask students to differentiate membrane and wall, RER and SER, chloroplasts and chromoplasts.
Osmosis experiments with cells, carrots and potato cups ask for explanations, hypotheses and controls.
Other questions cover organelle functions, DNA-containing organelles, bacterial versus animal cells, tumours and contact inhibition, and food preservation with salt and sugar.

bookSummary: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
Prokaryotic cells do not have a well-defined nucleus; their genetic material is in a region called the nucleoid, and they lack membrane-bound organelles.
Eukaryotic cells are larger and more complex, with a well-defined nucleus and several membrane-bound organelles.
All cells are surrounded by a cell membrane; cells of plants, fungi and bacteria also have a cell wall outside it.
The nucleus of eukaryotic cells contains chromosomes, composed of DNA and associated proteins, which carry genetic information.
All cells are filled with cytoplasm; in eukaryotic cells it contains several organelles, each with a specific function.
Important organelles include the nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, golgi apparatus, ribosomes and lysosomes.
Plant cells also contain plastids, such as chloroplasts, leucoplasts and chromoplasts.
Mitosis produces two daughter cells identical to the parent cell.
Meiosis is a two-step division producing four daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes.
Normal cells grow in a controlled manner, perform their functions and die naturally, while cancer cells keep dividing uncontrollably, forming tumours.

chapters.title: Tissues in Action
chapters.overview: The chapter explains tissues as groups of similar cells working together, and why plant and animal tissues differ. It covers meristematic tissues (apical, lateral, intercalary) and permanent tissues (epidermis, parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem, phloem) and plant tissue systems. It then describes animal tissues (epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous), the musculoskeletal system, types of joints and the skeletal system.

sections.title: Why are Plant and Animal Tissues Different?
points: Multicellular organisms have a hierarchy: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organism; tissues give division of labour.
Plants are mostly fixed and need rigid support from cell walls; animal cells lack walls, giving flexibility for locomotion.
Plants and animals differ in mode of nutrition, transport tissues and growth patterns.

sections.title: Tissues for Growth in Plants
points: Plants grow in length, in girth, and regrow after cutting or grazing.
This growth needs actively dividing cells forming meristematic tissue.

subsections.title: Apical meristem — How do plants grow in length?
points: Onion roots whose tips were cut stopped growing, while uncut roots kept growing.
Roots and shoots grow from their tips, where apical meristems contain continuously dividing cells.

subsections.title: Lateral meristem — How do plants grow in girth?
points: Stems of dicot plants increase in girth; annual growth rings on a cut trunk show a tree's age and past climatic conditions.
A ring of dividing cells in the stem, the lateral meristem, produces new cells inside and outside, increasing diameter.

subsections.title: Intercalary meristem — How do plants grow after being cut?
points: A cut stem stops growing in length but new branches arise from nodes; grass and hedges regrow after cutting.
Intercalary meristem lies at the base of the internode or just above the node.
Meristematic cells are small, thin-walled, with a large nucleus, dense cytoplasm, no vacuoles and no intercellular spaces.
Cells that lose the ability to divide become specialised permanent tissues through differentiation.

subsections.title: Permanent tissues
points: A T.S. of a sunflower stem shows different tissues, each specialised for a function; permanent tissues are simple or complex.
Epidermis: a single layer of tightly packed cells covered by a waxy cuticle; root hairs increase absorption and stomata allow gas exchange and transpiration.
Parenchyma: living, thin-walled, loosely packed cells that store food, photosynthesise, and form air spaces in aquatic plants.
Collenchyma: living cells with corners thickened by pectin, giving support and flexibility; sclerenchyma: mostly dead cells with lignified walls, hard and strong.
Xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres) carries water and minerals; phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres) carries food.
Plant tissues are organised into dermal, ground and vascular tissue systems; in older stems cork cambium forms dead cork cells making the bark.

sections.title: Animal Tissues
points: Animal cells group into tissues specially adapted to different functions like movement, sensing and holding the body together.

subsections.title: Epithelial tissues — Structure and functions
points: Epithelium covers the body and lines internal organs; its closely packed cells keep out germs and reduce water loss.
Single layer of thin flat cells for exchange (blood vessels, lungs); many layers for protection (skin, mouth, oesophagus).
Cuboidal or columnar cells for secretion (glands, stomach lining); receptor cells with cilia for senses; tall pillar-like cells for absorption (small intestine).

subsections.title: How are various parts connected in our body?
points: Connective tissue connects and supports other tissues; blood and bone are both connective tissues differing in their matrix.
Blood has plasma (55%) and formed elements (45%): RBCs with haemoglobin (live about 4 months), WBCs that fight infection and platelets that clot blood.
Bone has a rigid matrix of calcium and phosphorus compounds; cartilage is soft and flexible and cushions bone ends.
Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone and prevent excessive movement.

subsections.title: Can we control movement in our body?
points: Voluntary movements are made by skeletal muscles: long, cylindrical, unbranched, multinucleate, striated fibres.
Involuntary movements use smooth muscles: spindle-shaped, single nucleus, no striations, in stomach and intestines.
Cardiac muscles, only in the heart, are cylindrical, branched, single-nucleated with faint striations and work without fatigue.

subsections.title: How does the body sense, communicate and respond?
points: Nervous tissue forms the control and coordination network, with the brain as control centre; muscles act on its instructions.
Neurons have a cell body with nucleus, dendrites that receive signals, and an axon ending in axon terminals that transmit messages.

sections.title: The Musculoskeletal System
points: Made of bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments; helps us stand, move, keep posture and protect organs, under nervous control.
Muscles pull bones via tendons to produce movement at joints.
The adult skeleton is about 12–15 per cent of body weight; adult males have about 40–50 per cent muscle and females about 30–40 per cent.

subsections.title: The musculoskeletal system in action
points: Some body parts move in many directions and others in only one, because of the type of joint.
A joint is a junction between two or more bones; joints allow movement but cannot move bones on their own.

sections.title: Types of Joints
points: Joints are classified by the movement they allow.

subsections.title: Ball and socket joint
points: The rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into a hollow of the shoulder bone, allowing forward, backward, sideways and circular movement.

subsections.title: Hinge joint
points: The elbow and knee bend and straighten in one direction like a door hinge; the kneecap protects the knee joint.

subsections.title: Pivot joint
points: The skull joins the backbone through a pivot joint, letting the head turn side to side.

subsections.title: Fixed joints
points: Flat skull bones are joined by fixed joints that cannot move, keeping the brain safe; bone marrow stem cells are used in transplants for leukemia and thalassemia.

sections.title: Skeletal System
points: The skeleton of bones gives strength and protects organs; it includes skull, vertebral column and rib cage.
The vertebral column is a series of vertebrae with cartilage discs that cushion and allow bending without injuring the spinal cord.
Twelve pairs of ribs, joined to the spine and sternum by flexible cartilage, form a rib cage that expands and contracts in breathing.
Yoga, good posture, nutrition and exercise keep bones and muscles healthy; 21st June is International Yoga Day.
F. C. Steward (1958) regenerated whole carrot plants from single phloem cells, demonstrating totipotency; Agrobacterium tumefaciens causing crown gall is now used to introduce genes into plants.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Multiple-choice and assertion–reason questions on meristem cells, phloem, epithelium, cardiac muscle, tendons and hinge joints.

Reasoning questions on collenchyma flexibility, sugarcane cuttings with nodes, coconut husk sclerenchyma, meristem location and whether tissues have one function.

bookSummary: Tissues are groups of similar cells that work together to perform specific functions.
Different tissues coordinate with one another to perform life processes in plants and animals.
Plant tissues are broadly classified into meristematic and permanent tissues, depending on their ability to divide.
Functionally, plant tissues can be categorised as protecting, supporting and conducting tissue.
Permanent tissues may be simple (one type of cell) or complex (more than one type of cell).
Simple permanent tissues include parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
Complex permanent tissues include xylem and phloem, which transport water and food respectively.
Animal tissues are mainly of four types: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.
Epithelial tissue forms the outer covering of the body or protective lining of internal organs.
Connective tissue connects and supports various organs and tissues of the body.
Muscular tissue produces voluntary and involuntary movements.
Nervous tissue consists of neurons to receive and transmit impulses and helps regulate body activities.
Skeletal system protects organs and provides support.
Movement occurs by coordination of muscles and bones (musculoskeletal system) under the control of the nervous system.

chapters.title: Describing Motion Around Us
chapters.overview: The chapter describes motion in a straight line using position, distance travelled, displacement, average speed, average velocity and average acceleration. It shows how to plot and interpret position-time and velocity-time graphs, obtaining velocity and acceleration from slopes and displacement from areas. It derives the kinematic equations for constant acceleration, applies them to stopping distances, and introduces motion in a plane and uniform circular motion as accelerated motion.

sections.title: Motion in a Straight Line
points: Linear motion, or motion in a straight line, is the simplest kind of motion, e.g. a falling ball or a train on a straight track.
To discuss motion we first describe position at various instants of time.

subsections.title: Describing position
points: Position is the distance and direction of an object from a fixed reference point at an instant.
An object is in motion if its position relative to the reference point changes with time, and at rest otherwise.
On a straight line, positions right of the origin are generally positive and left are negative.

subsections.title: Distance travelled and displacement
points: An athlete running O to A (100 m) and back to B travels 160 m but has a displacement of 40 m in the positive direction.
Displacement is the net change in position between two instants; it needs magnitude and direction.
Total distance needs only a numerical value; the SI unit of both is the metre.
The magnitude of displacement is less than or equal to the distance travelled; they are equal if the object moves without turning back.
An instant of time is a single clock reading; a time interval is the duration between two readings.

subsections.title: Average speed and average velocity
points: Average speed = total distance travelled / time interval; it has no direction.
Uniform motion covers equal distances in equal time intervals; non-uniform motion covers unequal distances.
The idea of speed appears in the Aryabhatiya (5th century CE); a Ganitakaumudi (14th century CE) problem has two postmen meeting after 15 days.
Average velocity = displacement / time interval, with direction given by + or – sign; SI unit m s–1.
Rate of change is the ratio of change in a quantity to the corresponding change in time; a swimmer doing a 50 m round trip in 50 s has average speed 1 m s–1 and average velocity 0.

subsections.title: Average acceleration
points: Average acceleration = change in velocity / time interval, a = (v – u)/(t2 – t1); SI unit m s–2.
If speed increases, acceleration is in the direction of velocity; if it decreases, acceleration is opposite.
Acceleration can come from a change in magnitude or direction of velocity, or both.
A bus going from 10 to 15 m s–1 in 10 s has 0.5 m s–2; braking from 15 m s–1 to rest in 5 s gives –3 m s–2.
A dropped object gains 9.8 m s–1 each second; this constant acceleration due to the Earth's gravitational force is g.

sections.title: Graphical Representation of Motion
points: Graphs visually show how position, velocity and acceleration change with time and help compare motions.
Graphs in the chapter are for straight-line motion in one direction, where distance equals magnitude of displacement.

subsections.title: Plotting graph
points: Draw X and Y axes meeting at origin O, choose which quantity goes on each axis, and choose suitable scales.
Plot each time–position pair and join the points; constant speed gives a straight line, speeding up gives a curve.
A graph is not a route map; it shows how position changes with time.

subsections.title: Position-time graphs
points: A straight-line position-time graph means constant velocity; a curved graph means changing velocity (accelerated motion).
The slope BC/CA of the position-time line gives the average velocity.
A line parallel to the time axis means the object is at rest.
A steeper slope means a higher velocity.

subsections.title: Velocity-time graphs
points: A line parallel to the time axis means constant velocity and zero acceleration.
A straight rising line means velocity increasing with constant acceleration; a straight falling line means decreasing velocity with constant acceleration opposite to velocity.
The slope of a velocity-time line gives acceleration (e.g. 0.5 m s–2 and –0.5 m s–2).
The area between the line and the time axis gives displacement (e.g. 20 m s–1 × 6 s = 120 m; a trapezium area of 75 m).

sections.title: Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration
points: From the definition of acceleration, v = u + at.
The area under the velocity-time graph gives s = ut + ½at².
Eliminating t gives v² = u² + 2as; these kinematic equations are valid only for constant acceleration.
With braking acceleration –4 m s–2, a car stops in 28.1 m from 54 km h–1 but 112.5 m from 108 km h–1.
Stopping distance depends on speed, road surface, braking capacity and reaction time, so a safe distance must be kept; V2V communication warns of collisions.

sections.title: Motion in a Plane
points: Motion in a plane, like overtaking, a kicked ball or a satellite's circular path, is motion in two dimensions; motion in space is three-dimensional.

subsections.title: Uniform circular motion
points: In one revolution of radius R the distance is 2πR and the displacement is zero; average speed = 2πR/T.
Uniform circular motion is motion in a circular path at constant speed.
A track with ever more sides approaches a circle, where the direction of velocity changes continuously.
A marble released from a ring moves in a straight line; velocity at a point is along the tangent to the circle.
Uniform circular motion is accelerated because the direction of velocity changes; it is an idealised model for planets and vehicles turning.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Numerical problems on distance and displacement, average acceleration, stopping distance and reaction time.
Interpreting position-time and velocity-time graphs, shading areas for displacement, and plotting graphs for two cars.
Conceptual questions on accelerating at constant speedometer reading, rest on a moving Earth, and the minute hand of a clock.

keyTerms.meaning: A fixed point with respect to which the position of an object is described.

An object is in motion if its position with respect to the reference point changes with time; at rest if it does not.

keyTerms.term: Instant of time and time interval
keyTerms.meaning: An instant is a single clock reading; a time interval is the duration between two readings.
Scalars are specified by numerical value alone; vectors need both direction and magnitude.
Total distance travelled divided by the time interval in which it is covered.

keyTerms.term: Uniform motion in a straight line
keyTerms.meaning: Travelling equal distances in equal intervals of time; non-uniform motion covers unequal distances.
Displacement divided by the time interval in which it occurs; the average rate of change of position.
The ratio of change in one quantity to the corresponding change in time.
The fixed value average velocity approaches as the time interval becomes infinitesimally small.
Change in velocity divided by the time interval.
Acceleration due to the gravitational force by the Earth, 9.8 m s–2.
The steepness of a line; the rate of change of the Y-axis quantity with respect to the X-axis quantity.
Equations relating s, t, u, v and a for straight-line motion with constant acceleration.
Motion in a plane.
Motion of an object in a circular path with constant (uniform) speed.
A straight line that meets the circle at one and only one point.

If the position of the object with respect to a reference point changes with time, the object is said to be in motion.
Displacement is the net change in the position of the object between two given instants of time.
The average speed of an object is the total distance travelled divided by the time interval during which this distance is covered.
The average velocity of an object in a time interval is the change in position (displacement) divided by the time interval.
The average acceleration of an object over a time interval is the change in its velocity divided by the time interval.

chapters.title: Exploring Mixtures and their Separation
chapters.overview: The chapter classifies mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous and as solutions, suspensions or colloids. It explains the concentration of solutions as mass by mass, mass by volume and volume by volume percentages, solubility and solubility curves. It describes separation methods for homogeneous mixtures (crystallization, distillation, paper chromatography) and heterogeneous mixtures (separating funnel, sublimation, centrifugation, coagulation), and uses the Tyndall effect to distinguish colloids and suspensions from solutions.

sections.title: How Can We Classify Mixtures?
points: A homogeneous mixture or solution, like sugar in water, vinegar or soda, has uniform composition throughout.
A heterogeneous mixture, like sand in water, is not uniform and its particles may be visible and settle.
Salt, chalk powder and milk in water behave differently when a laser beam passes through and when filtered, showing different types of mixtures.

sections.title: Solutions
points: A solution forms when a solute (substance dissolved) is mixed with a solvent (substance that dissolves it).

subsections.title: Concentration of a solution
points: ORS and pesticide sprays need specified proportions of solute and solvent; too little or too much causes problems.
Concentration is the amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent or solution.
Dilip Mahalanabis formulated ORS, which WHO popularised worldwide.

subsections.title: How do we express concentration?
points: Mass by mass percentage: grams of solute in 100 g of solution; used for packaged foods and also heterogeneous mixtures like milk powder.
Mass by volume percentage: grams of solute in 100 mL of solution, e.g. 5% glucose, 0.9% m/v saline drip.
Volume by volume percentage: mL of solute in 100 mL of solution, used for miscible liquids like vinegar and perfumes.
Worked examples: 10 g salt in 90 g water is 10% m/m; 5 g glucose in 100 mL is 5% m/v; 1 mL pesticide in 100 mL is 1% v/v.

subsections.title: Solubility of substances
points: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed quantity of solvent at a given temperature; such a solution is saturated.
Solubility of solids in liquids generally increases with temperature; that of gases in liquids generally decreases.
A solubility curve plots solubility against temperature; compound B dissolves 287 g per 100 g water at 60 °C and 241 g at 40 °C.

sections.title: Methods of Separation of Homogeneous Mixtures
points: Homogeneous mixtures are separated using differences in solubility, boiling point and interaction with a solvent and paper.

subsections.title: Crystallization
points: Cooling a saturated solution makes excess solute separate as pure crystals, solids with particles in a regular geometric pattern.
Crystallization separates and purifies solids, based on differences in solubility at different temperatures.
Copper sulfate crystals are made by saturating a hot solution, filtering it and cooling slowly; slow cooling gives larger crystals.
Salt is obtained from seawater; Indian coastal communities made panga salt by boiling brine and karkatch salt by evaporation.

subsections.title: Distillation
points: Distillation heats a mixture until the lower-boiling liquid vaporises, then cools the vapour in a condenser back to liquid.
It separates miscible liquids differing in boiling point by at least about 25 °C, or recovers a liquid from dissolved solids.
Acetone (about 56 °C) and water (100 °C) can be separated by distillation.
Kannauj makes Mitti ka Ittar by the traditional Deg-Bhapka distillation method.
Fractional distillation separates liquids with boiling points differing by less than 25 °C, e.g. crude petroleum into petroleum gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel and bitumen.

subsections.title: Paper Chromatography
points: A black sketch-pen spot on paper dipped in water separates into different colours as water rises.
Paper chromatography separates components by their different interactions with the solvent and paper, so they move at different rates.
Pigments of spinach or flower petals can be separated; some need alcohol or mixed solvents.
'Chromatography' comes from Greek chroma (colour) and graphein (to write).

sections.title: How Can We Separate the Components of Heterogeneous Mixtures?
points: Heterogeneous mixtures are separated using properties such as density, sublimation and particle size.

subsections.title: Separation of two immiscible liquids
points: Immiscible liquids like oil and water form separate layers.
In a separating funnel, mustard oil forms the upper layer; water is drained through the stopcock and the oil collected separately.
Most gas mixtures are homogeneous; smoke, fog and dust in air are heterogeneous mixtures with a gas component.

subsections.title: Sublimation
points: Heating camphor and sand under an inverted funnel deposits camphor on the funnel while sand remains.
Sublimation is a solid changing directly to vapour below its melting point; deposition is vapour changing directly back to solid.
Naphthalene and dry ice also sublime.
An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of metals, or a metal and non-metal, that cannot be separated physically, e.g. brass, bronze, stainless steel.

subsections.title: Suspensions
points: Suspensions are heterogeneous mixtures whose insoluble particles, larger than solution particles and visible, remain suspended.
Filtration may not clear muddy water fully, so centrifugation or coagulation is used.
Centrifugation spins a mixture at high speed so heavier particles settle at the bottom; used to separate blood components; a hand-powered paperfuge works without electricity.
Coagulation uses a coagulant like alum to clump fine particles, which settle by sedimentation and are removed by decantation or filtration; paneer formation also involves coagulation.

subsections.title: Colloids
points: Blood, milk, tomato sauce and ice cream are colloids, neither solutions nor true suspensions.
Solution particles are less than 1 nm, colloid particles 1–1000 nm and suspension particles more than 1000 nm.
Colloid particles do not settle and are uniformly dispersed; donated blood is separated into plasma, platelets and cells.

sections.title: Tyndall Effect
points: The laser path was invisible in salt solution but visible in chalk suspension and milk mixture because particles scattered light.
Scattering of light by particles is the Tyndall effect, first explained by John Tyndall; seen in beams through a small hole or stadium floodlights.
A colloid has a dispersed phase and a dispersion medium; emulsions have both as liquids (oil-in-water like milk, water-in-oil like butter), stabilised by emulsifying agents.
Separation relies on size, density and solubility; sewage treatment, waste segregation and recovering lithium from batteries apply these ideas.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Classifying mixtures, identifying those showing the Tyndall effect and completing a table of solutions, suspensions and colloids.
Concentration calculations for a cake mix, brass and sugar solutions, and solubility table questions.
Choosing and justifying separation methods for given mixtures, including distillation set-ups and a sand–salt–naphthalene mixture.

A substance that stabilises an emulsion, e.g. proteins in milk and butter.

Separation of mixtures is a crucial process for obtaining pure substances.
Crystallization is a technique used to get a pure solid from its saturated solution.
Distillation is used to separate two miscible liquids with a minimum difference of 25 °C in boiling points; it can also obtain a liquid from a mixture of a liquid and a solid.
Paper chromatography separates compounds using differences in their rates of movement on the paper.
A separating funnel is used to separate two immiscible liquids based on their different densities.

Centrifugation uses rapid spinning to separate heavier solid particles from a solid-liquid mixture.
Coagulation involves adding a coagulant to make smaller particles clump together and settle in a heterogeneous mixture of solids and liquids.
The dispersed particles in a colloid or suspension scatter light, which is known as the Tyndall effect.

chapters.title: How Forces Affect Motion
chapters.overview: The chapter investigates what causes changes in motion. It treats force as a quantity with magnitude and direction, distinguishes balanced and unbalanced forces and net force, and studies friction experimentally. It then states and applies Newton's three laws of motion, including F = ma, weight F = mg, applications like catching a ball, airbags and rockets, and treating connected objects as a single system.

sections.title: The Concept of Force
points: A force can move an object from rest, change its speed or direction, and change its shape.
Force needs direction as well as magnitude and unit; the SI unit is the newton (N).
Changing the magnitude or direction of a force changes its effect.

subsections.title: Measuring the magnitude of a force
points: A spring balance measures weight, the gravitational force of the Earth on an object, and force in general.
The smallest forces we can feel are millinewtons; scientists can measure down to yoctonewtons (10–24 N).

sections.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
points: Usually more than one force acts on an object, e.g. push and friction, or gravity and buoyant force.
Equal and opposite forces are balanced; in tug of war with equal pulls the rope does not move.
For opposite unequal forces the net force is their difference along the larger force; for forces in the same direction it is their sum.
Forces of 10 N and 6 N give a net force of 16 N or 4 N depending on their directions; equal and opposite forces on ends of an extended object can make it rotate.

sections.title: The Force of Friction: Often Overlooked but Always Present
points: A box moves only when the applied force exceeds friction between it and the floor; weight and normal force on it are balanced.
A moving object slows and stops when the push stops because friction acts opposite to motion.
A coin stack launched by a rubber band travels farther on smoother surfaces; a spring balance shows friction is smaller there.
With smaller friction, velocity decreases more slowly and the object travels farther; a thought experiment with zero friction suggests motion continues forever.
Galileo in the 17th century argued that a body with all impediments removed would move indefinitely.

sections.title: Newton’s First Law of Motion
points: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues with constant velocity, unless a net force acts on it.
Newton used 'inertia' for the tendency of objects to resist change in their state; he presented the three laws in 1687.
A box pushed with a force equal to friction has zero net force and keeps moving at constant velocity.
With no net force, position-time graphs are flat or straight lines and velocity-time graphs are horizontal lines.

sections.title: Newton’s Second Law of Motion
points: A cart pulled by a falling cup accelerates more when the pulling force is doubled and less when the cart's mass is doubled.
The acceleration is in the direction of the net force, proportional to it and inversely proportional to mass: a = F/m, F = ma.
One newton gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s–2; gravitational force on mass m is F = mg with g = 9.8 m s–2.
The complete form states that the rate of change of momentum (mass × velocity) is proportional to the net force.
Pulling hands back when catching, airbags and cushioning increase stopping time, reducing acceleration and force; a coconut hitting the ground stops quickly, so a large force breaks it.

sections.title: Newton’s Third Law of Motion
points: Pushing a table from a wheeled chair moves you the opposite way; two connected spring balances show equal readings.
Whenever one object exerts a force on a second, the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first; the pair acts on different objects.
Walking, climbing trees, rowing a canoe, a balloon on a string and a rocket launch are explained by the third law; friction helps us walk.
The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 fired its engine in its direction of motion to slow down for a soft landing.
The law holds for non-contact forces too; equal forces give unequal accelerations for unequal masses, as with the Earth and a fruit or a gun's recoil.

sections.title: Forces Acting on a System of Objects
points: Two boxes joined by a string and pulled by force F can be treated as one system.
Tension between the boxes is an internal force and need not be considered; only external forces matter.
The system accelerates like a single object: a = F/(m1 + m2).
Newton's laws need modification only near very massive objects, at speeds near light, and at atomic scales.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Questions on friction at constant velocity, net force on blocks and a snake boat, and identifying net force from graphs.
Applications of the third law: a sailor jumping from a boat, colliding carts, a magnet and compass.
Numerical problems on stopping force on a bullet, time of contact in a kick, distance on a rough patch, and combined accelerations of a tractor load.

SI unit of force; the force that produces an acceleration of 1 m s–2 on a mass of 1 kg.
The gravitational force with which the Earth pulls an object.
Forces equal in magnitude but opposite in direction acting on an object.
The combined effect of forces on an object; non-zero when forces are unbalanced.
Force between surfaces in contact acting opposite to the direction of motion.
Force exerted by a surface on an object placed on it, acting upward perpendicular to the surface.
An experiment carried out in imagination when conditions are difficult to recreate in the real world.
The tendency of objects to resist change in their state of rest or uniform motion.
The product of an object's mass and velocity, in the direction of velocity.
Acceleration of a falling object due to the Earth, 9.8 m s–2, independent of the object's mass.
The force applied by a string between connected objects.
Forces within a system, and forces acting on the system from outside.

chapters.title: Work, Energy, and Simple Machines
chapters.overview: The chapter defines work done by a constant force, including zero, positive and negative work, and links work to energy through the work-energy theorem. It introduces forms of energy, derives kinetic energy ½mv² and gravitational potential energy mgh, and shows conservation of mechanical energy with a falling object and a pendulum. It then defines power and explains simple machines — pulleys, inclined planes and levers — through mechanical advantage.

sections.title: Work Done by a Constant Force
points: Lifting three bags, or one bag three times as high, takes three times the work: work grows with force and with distance.
Work done by a constant force = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = F × s.
The SI unit of work is the joule: 1 J = 1 N × 1 m = 1 kg m² s–2.
Work equals the area under a force-displacement graph, even for a changing force; the force (agency) and the object must be specified.

subsections.title: When is work done equal to zero?
points: Work is zero if the force is zero or if there is no displacement, as when pushing a rigid wall, even though muscles tire.
A force perpendicular to displacement, like carrying a box while walking, does no work.

subsections.title: Positive and negative work done
points: Work is positive when displacement is in the direction of force (pushing a wheelchair) and negative when opposite (a goalkeeper stopping a ball).
Work has no direction, only a positive or negative sign.
A goalkeeper's 200 N force over 15 cm backward does –30 J of work on the ball.

sections.title: The Work-Energy Theorem
points: An object having the capacity to do work possesses energy; a thrown ball or a raised pot gains energy from work done on it.
Work done on an object = change in its energy; this holds for systems and variable forces too. Energy's SI unit is the joule.
Energy is also transferred as heat, radiation, electric circuits, sound waves and nuclear reactions.
In a carrom shot, each striking coin does positive work on the next and receives equal negative work.

sections.title: Forms of Energy
points: Energy exists as mechanical, electrical, thermal, light, sound, chemical and nuclear energy.
Energy changes form: electrical to light in a bulb, chemical in food to mechanical in muscles, mechanical to sound in a bell.

sections.title: Mechanical Energy
points: Mechanical energy is the energy an object possesses due to its motion or position.

subsections.title: Kinetic energy
points: Kinetic energy is energy due to motion; an object at rest has zero kinetic energy.
Using v² = u² + 2as and F = ma, the work done is W = ½m(v² – u²), so K = ½mv².
Positive work increases kinetic energy and negative work decreases it; doubling velocity makes it four times.
A 0.2 kg ball at 43 m s–1 has 184.9 J; a jet stopped by a deck wire must have landed at 70 m s–1.

subsections.title: Potential energy
points: A stretched band, bent bow or compressed spring stores the work done in deforming it and gives it to objects on release.
Separated magnets, electric charges, or a ball and the Earth store energy due to their relative positions.
Potential energy is energy stored due to deformation or relative positions of objects in a system.

subsections.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
points: A ball dropped from greater heights makes deeper depressions in sand, showing greater potential energy.
Raising mass m to height h needs work mgh, so U = mgh; this expression is valid only near the Earth's surface.
Work against friction does not store energy.

subsections.title: Conservation of mechanical energy
points: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy.
For a freely falling object the loss in potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy (½mg²t²), so mechanical energy stays mgh.
A pendulum bob swings back to almost its starting height; it eventually stops due to friction and air resistance.
A child reaching the bottom of a slide of height h has v = √(2gh), independent of mass and slide shape; energy methods also size a truck escape ramp (20 m).

sections.title: Power
points: Power is the rate at which work is done: P = W/t.
The SI unit is the watt: 1 W = 1 J s–1; one horsepower is 746 W.
Lifting 75 kg by 2 m in 5 s needs 300 W; a 1000 kg car reaching 20 m s–1 in 10 s needs 20000 W.

sections.title: Simple Machines
points: Simple machines make tasks easier by changing the magnitude or direction of the force, not by reducing total work.
Effort is the force applied; load is the force to be overcome; mechanical advantage = load/effort.

subsections.title: Pulley
points: A pulley is a grooved wheel guiding a rope; a fixed pulley only changes the direction of effort, so its mechanical advantage is 1.
Movable pulleys or pulley systems give mechanical advantage greater than 1 and are used in elevators and cranes.

subsections.title: Inclined plane
points: Pulling a cart up a plank needs less force than lifting it, and less still on a less steep plank, but over a longer distance.
Ignoring friction, F′ × L = mgh, so mechanical advantage = L/h, greater than 1.
A ramp 50 cm long over a 30 cm step has mechanical advantage 1.67.

subsections.title: Lever
points: A lever is a rigid bar rotating about a fixed point; its parts are fulcrum, load and effort, with load arm and effort arm.
Work transferred along the lever gives F1 × d1 = F2 × d2.
A beam balance shows effort × effort arm = load × load arm; mechanical advantage = effort arm/load arm.
Class I levers have the fulcrum in between, Class II the load in between, Class III the effort in between.
Machines do not create energy; perpetual motion machines do not work. Watermills (gharat) and dams convert water's potential energy to kinetic energy.

points: True/false and fill-in-the-blank questions on work, energy and power, and a ball at its highest point.
Identifying energy transformations and path-independence of potential energy.
Numerical problems on cranes, scooters, a seesaw, air resistance, variable force graphs, the Moon, braking cars and a falling coconut.

An object having capacity to do work is said to possess energy.
Work-energy theorem: Work done on an object or a system is equal to the change in its energy.
The energy possessed by an object due to its motion is called kinetic energy.
The energy stored by an object as a result of its deformation or in a system of objects due to their relative positions is called potential energy.
Power is defined as the rate at which work is done.
Simple machines are devices that make work easier by changing the magnitude or direction of the force that needs to be applied, though they do not reduce total work.

chapters.title: Journey Inside the Atom
chapters.overview: The chapter traces the idea of the atom from Acharya Kanada and the Greek atomists to Dalton's theory, and follows the historical atomic models of Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr with the discoveries of the electron, proton and neutron. It introduces symbols of elements, atomic number, mass number and the distribution of electrons in shells for the first eighteen elements. It explains valency, isotopes and their uses, weighted average atomic mass, and isobars.

sections.title: Rediscovering the Roots of Atomic Theory
points: Acharya Kanada held that repeatedly divided matter (dravya) reaches indivisible parmanus, which combine as dyads and triads; recorded in the Vaisesika Sutras.
Leucippus and Democritus called indivisible particles atomos; the early concept was an imaginary idea, not experimental.
In 1808 John Dalton proposed his experimentally based atomic theory: all matter is made of indivisible atoms.
Scientists then asked what atoms are made of and what makes atoms of different elements differ.

sections.title: A Short Historical Journey Through Atomic Models
points: Atomic models were changed and improved as new evidence appeared, showing how science progresses.
Radioactivity showed atoms are made of smaller particles.

In 1897 J. J. Thomson found cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles (electrons), much lighter than atoms and present in all elements; the electron's charge (–1.602 × 10–19 C) is taken as –1.

subsections.title: Thomson’s model of an atom
points: Thomson proposed the atom as a sphere of positive charge with electrons distributed throughout, the plum pudding model.
A watermelon is a familiar picture: red pulp as positive matter and seeds as electrons.
It was the first genuine attempt to describe how positive and negative charges balance.

subsections.title: Testing Thomson’s model: The gold foil experiment
points: In 1911 Geiger and Marsden, under Rutherford, fired alpha particles (helium nuclei) at a very thin gold foil.
Most passed undeflected, some were sharply deflected and a few bounced back; this deflection is called scattering.
Thomson's model could not explain these results.

subsections.title: Rutherford’s model of an atom
points: Most of an atom is empty space; a tiny dense nucleus holds all positive charge and most of the mass.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus like planets: the planetary model.
The atom is about 10–10 m across and the nucleus about 10–15 m, about 10⁵ times smaller.

subsections.title: Limitations of Rutherford’s model
points: An electron moving in a circle is accelerating and should lose energy, spiral inward and fall into the nucleus.
Atoms are actually stable, so the model could not explain stability.

subsections.title: Discovery of the proton
points: Rutherford showed the nucleus's positive charge comes from protons, much heavier than electrons with equal and opposite charge.
In a neutral atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons (helium 2 and 2, sodium 11 and 11).

subsections.title: Bohr’s model of the atom
points: In 1913 Bohr proposed that electrons move in fixed orbits (stationary states, shells, energy levels) K, L, M, N or n = 1, 2, 3, 4.
An electron in an allowed shell does not lose energy; K is closest to the nucleus with least energy, and energy increases outward.
Electrons change shells by absorbing or releasing energy equal to the difference between levels; each shell holds a limited number.
The K, L, M naming came from Charles Barkla's X-ray lines; the later quantum mechanical model replaced Bohr's.

sections.title: What Components Contribute to the Mass of an Atom?
points: Electrons are so light their mass can be ignored; helium has two protons but about four times hydrogen's mass.

subsections.title: Discovery of the Neutron
points: In 1932 James Chadwick discovered the neutron, with mass nearly equal to a proton and no charge.
Neutrons are in the nucleus of all atoms except hydrogen; atomic mass comes mainly from protons and neutrons.
Heavier atoms have more neutrons than protons (iron 26 and 30, uranium 92 and 146); neutrons reduce proton repulsion and strengthen the nuclear force.
BARC in Mumbai uses the Dhruva reactor for neutron-scattering research.

sections.title: Symbols of Elements
points: Dalton introduced pictorial symbols in 1803; in 1813 Berzelius suggested alphabetic symbols from Latin names.
IUPAC approves names and symbols; a symbol's first letter is uppercase and any second letter lowercase (Al, Co).
Some symbols use a letter other than the second (Cl, Zn) or come from Latin, Greek or German names (Fe, Hg, W).
About 69 elements were known by 1869; 118 are known today.

sections.title: Atomic Number
points: The atomic number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus; it determines the element's identity and chemical behaviour.
In a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons (hydrogen 1, helium 2).

sections.title: Mass Number
points: The mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) in the nucleus.
Electron mass is negligible and ignored in calculations.
An atom is written with the mass number as superscript and atomic number as subscript before the symbol, e.g. carbon-12 with Z = 6.

sections.title: How Are Electrons Distributed in Different Energy Levels?
points: Bohr–Bury rules: a shell holds at most 2n² electrons (K 2, L 8, M 18).
The outermost shell holds at most 8 electrons.
Shells fill stepwise from the nucleus outward, K before L before M.

subsections.title: Building up atoms
points: Adding one electron for each increase in atomic number builds the structures of the first eighteen elements.
The distribution of electrons among shells is the electronic configuration, e.g. sodium 2, 8, 1 and argon 2, 8, 8.

sections.title: Combining Capacity of an Atom: Valency
points: Combining capacity is the number of hydrogen or chlorine atoms one atom combines with, e.g. oxygen in H2O is two.
The outermost shell is the valence shell and its electrons are valence electrons; 8 electrons form an octet.
Atoms with a complete octet (or 2 for helium) are stable and unreactive; others lose, gain or share electrons.
Valency is the number of electrons gained, lost or shared to complete the octet: sodium 1, oxygen 2, carbon 4.

sections.title: A Deeper Look into Atomic Structure
points: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons.

subsections.title: Isotopes
points: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, e.g. protium, deuterium and tritium; carbon-12, 13 and 14.
Isotopes have similar chemical properties (same electronic configuration) but different physical properties.
Uses: uranium-235 as nuclear fuel, cobalt-60 for cancer treatment, iodine-131 for goitre, carbon-14 for dating fossils.
Atomic masses are measured in unified atomic mass units (u).

subsections.title: Average atomic mass
points: Chlorine has isotopes of 35 u and 37 u in the ratio 3:1; a simple average (36 u) ignores abundance.
The weighted average atomic mass multiplies each isotope's mass by its percentage abundance: chlorine is 35.5 u.

subsections.title: Isobars
points: Calcium (20), potassium (19) and argon (18) all have mass number 40.
Atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers are isobars.
Electrons are now understood as electron clouds rather than fixed orbits; STMs and TEMs image atoms.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Evaluating statements about the gold foil experiment and Bohr's model, and ordering the atomic models chronologically.
Relating atomic species as isotopes or isobars, and calculating protons, neutrons and electrons.
Electronic configuration, valency and the effect of hypothetical heavier electrons on an atom.

bookSummary: Atoms are the building blocks of matter.
J. J. Thomson proposed that in an atom, electrons are embedded in a positively charged sphere.
Rutherford’s model described the atom as mostly empty space, with a dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre and electrons orbiting it.
Niels Bohr’s model proposed that electrons move in fixed energy levels (shells) around the nucleus.
The shells of an atom are named as K, L, M, N, and so on.
James Chadwick discovered the presence of neutrons in the atom.
The three subatomic particles of an atom are electrons, protons and neutrons.
If the outermost shell has an octet of electrons (or two in case of helium), the atom is stable and largely unreactive.
Valency is the combining capacity of an atom, equal to the number of electrons gained, lost or shared to achieve a stable configuration.
The atomic number of an element is equal to the number of protons in its nucleus.
The mass number of an atom is equal to the total number of nucleons (protons and neutrons) in its nucleus.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
The average atomic mass of an element is calculated based on the relative abundance of its isotopes in nature.
Isobars are atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

chapters.title: Atomic Foundations of Matter
chapters.overview: The chapter shows experimentally that mass is conserved in physical and chemical changes and states the Laws of Conservation of Mass and Constant Proportions, which led to Dalton's atomic theory. It explains how atoms combine by sharing electrons (covalent bonds) or transferring electrons (ionic bonds), how covalent and ionic compounds are named, and how chemical formulae are written by criss-crossing valencies. It compares properties of ionic and covalent compounds and calculates molecular mass and formula unit mass.

sections.title: Law of Conservation of Mass
points: Dissolving salt in water does not change total mass; this holds for all physical changes.
Baking soda and vinegar lose mass in an open flask because carbon dioxide escapes, but not when a balloon traps the gas.
Matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; proposed by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789.
Sodium sulfate and barium chloride form barium sulfate precipitate and sodium chloride with no change in total mass.
Worked examples: reactants of 6.92 g give 6.92 g of products; 2.4 g of carbon gives 8.8 g of carbon dioxide.

sections.title: Law of Constant Proportions
points: Joseph Proust proposed that elements in a compound combine in a fixed ratio by mass, irrespective of source.
Purified water from any source contains hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1:8.
Cinnabar (hingula) yields mercury and sulfur in about 86.22% and 13.78% by mass.
Sodium chloride has sodium and chlorine in the ratio 23:35.5, so 46 g sodium needs 71 g chlorine.

sections.title: Dalton’s Atomic Theory
points: The two laws formed the basis of Dalton's theory; atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in reactions.
A postulate is a fundamental assumption accepted as truth without formal proof.
Dalton postulated that matter is made of atoms that are indivisible, identical for one element and different for different elements.
Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios, and the relative number and kinds of atoms in a compound are constant.

sections.title: How Atoms Combine?
points: A molecule is an electrically neutral entity of more than one atom capable of independent existence and showing all properties of the substance.
Some elements, like helium, exist only as atoms.
Atoms combine by sharing or transferring valence electrons, lowering the total energy and becoming more stable.
The force that holds atoms together is a chemical bond.

subsections.title: Bonding by sharing of electrons — Covalent Bond
points: Two hydrogen atoms share one electron each to form H2; a shared electron pair is a covalent bond, and one shared pair is a single bond (H—H).
Chlorine atoms share one electron each (Cl—Cl); oxygen atoms share two electrons each, forming a double bond (O=O).

subsections.title: Molecules of compounds
points: Hydrogen and chlorine share one electron each to form HCl, a covalent compound.
Two hydrogen atoms each share an electron with one oxygen atom to form H2O.
Nuclear energy from splitting or combining nuclei generates electricity; Raja Ramanna contributed to India's nuclear programme.

subsections.title: Naming covalent compounds
points: Prefixes mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa- give numbers of atoms; the second element ends in -ide.
Mono- is omitted for the first element; a final 'o' or 'a' is dropped before a vowel (monoxide, pentoxide).
Examples: CO carbon monoxide, CS2 carbon disulfide, PCl3 phosphorus trichloride, SF6 sulfur hexafluoride, N2O4 dinitrogen tetroxide.
No prefix is used before hydrogen (H2S hydrogen sulfide); water and ammonia keep common names.

subsections.title: Bonding by electron transfer — Ionic bond
points: Sodium loses its single valence electron to become the cation Na+; chlorine gains one electron to become the chloride anion Cl–.
Cations and anions are ions; the electrostatic attraction holding oppositely charged ions together is an ionic bond.
Ionic compounds form 3-D crystals; in NaCl each ion is surrounded by six ions of opposite charge, shown as a crystal lattice.

subsections.title: Naming ionic compounds
points: The cation is named first, then the anion; simple anion names end in -ide.
Metals generally form cations and non-metals anions.
Polyatomic ions contain two or more elements and generally do not end in -ide, e.g. hydroxide, nitrate, carbonate, sulfate, ammonium.

sections.title: Writing Chemical Formulae
points: Formulae can be written quickly by criss-crossing valencies or charges.

subsections.title: Writing chemical formulae of covalent compounds
points: Write the symbols, write their valencies, and cross them over as subscripts; a subscript of one is not written.
Examples: HCl, H2S, CCl4.

subsections.title: Writing chemical formulae of ionic compounds
points: Write cation then anion, put charges below, criss-cross the numbers and divide by any common factor.
Examples: CaCl2, Al2O3, MgO (not Mg2O2), CaCO3.
Brackets are used for two or more of the same polyatomic ion: Mg(OH)2, Al(OH)3, Al2(SO4)3; charges are not shown in the formula.

sections.title: Properties of the Ionic and the Covalent Compounds
points: Ionic compounds like sodium chloride and copper sulfate are generally soluble in water but not in kerosene or petrol; covalent compounds like camphor and naphthalene are the reverse.
Ionic compounds do not conduct in the solid state because ions are fixed, but conduct when dissolved in water.
Sugar dissolves in water but gives no ions and does not conduct electricity.
Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points; covalent compounds usually low.

sections.title: Molecular Mass of Covalent Compounds
points: Molecular mass is found by adding the masses of all atoms in the molecule.
Ionic compounds form crystals, not molecules.

sections.title: Formula Unit Mass of Ionic Compounds
points: A formula unit is the simplest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound; its mass is the formula unit mass.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Predicting ions, bond types and formulae from electron arrangements.
Writing formulae and names of compounds, completing an ion table, and calculating formula unit masses.
Verifying conservation of mass numerically and analysing species with given protons, neutrons and electrons.

A fundamental assumption accepted as truth without formal proof from which further ideas are developed.

The force that holds atoms together.
Interaction between atoms through a shared pair of electrons.
Atoms joined by one shared electron pair, or by two shared pairs.
A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons, e.g. Na+.
A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains electrons, e.g. Cl–.
Cations and anions collectively.
The electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions that holds them together.
Regular repeating 3-D arrangement of ions; the lattice depicts ions as points.
Ions formed by a combination of atoms of two or more elements.
Total mass of a molecule, the sum of atomic masses of its atoms.
The simplest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound.
The mass of a formula unit; sum of atomic masses of its atoms.

keyResults.label: Law of Conservation of Mass
keyResults.statement: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction (Lavoisier, 1789).

keyResults.label: Law of Constant Proportions
keyResults.statement: A compound always contains the same elements combined in a fixed ratio by mass, e.g. hydrogen : oxygen in water = 1 : 8.

keyResults.label: Dalton’s postulates
keyResults.statement: Matter is made of indivisible atoms that are not created or destroyed; atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties; atoms of different elements differ; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios; relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a compound.

keyResults.label: Properties
keyResults.statement: Ionic compounds: soluble in water, conduct in solution not as solids, high melting and boiling points; covalent compounds: often insoluble in water, non-conducting, low melting and boiling points.

bookSummary: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. This is known as the Law of Conservation of Mass.
A compound always contains the same elements combined in a fixed ratio by mass, no matter how it is formed or where it is obtained. This is called the Law of Definite Proportions.
A molecule is an electrically neutral entity of more than one atom that can exist independently and shows all its chemical properties.
Atoms combine to form molecules of elements or compounds to become stable; they are held together by a chemical bond.
A covalent bond is formed by the sharing of electrons between atoms.
An ionic bond is formed by the transfer of electrons between atoms, forming cations and anions.
The chemical formula of a covalent compound represents the elements and number of atoms of each element present in it.
The chemical formula of an ionic compound represents the simplest whole number ratio of atoms of different elements present in it.
Molecular mass is the total mass of a molecule, calculated by adding the atomic masses of all its atoms.
Formula unit mass of an ionic compound is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in a formula unit.

chapters.title: Sound Waves: Characteristics and Applications
chapters.overview: The chapter explains that sound is produced by vibrations and needs a medium, travelling as a longitudinal mechanical wave of compressions and rarefactions that carries energy. It represents sound waves graphically and defines wavelength, frequency, time period, amplitude, intensity and speed (v = νλ), and relates pitch and loudness to frequency and amplitude. It covers reflection of sound (echo, reverberation) and uses of infrasonic and ultrasonic waves, including echolocation and sonar.

sections.title: Production of Sound
points: A plucked rubber band makes sound only while it vibrates, so sound is produced by vibrations (periodic to and fro motion).
Strings, membranes and air columns vibrate in musical instruments; the object producing sound is the source.
Humans produce sound by vibrating vocal cords in the larynx; grasshoppers and crickets rub wings or legs.

subsections.title: Tuning fork
points: A tuning fork is a U-shaped metal bar with a stem; its prongs vibrate when struck on a rubber pad.
A vibrating prong touching water makes waves, confirming that sound comes from vibrating objects.
In Kongthong, Meghalaya, each person has a tune name (Jingrwai Iawbei).

sections.title: Propagation of Sound
points: Sound knocked on a desk is heard through the desk, and spoons tapped under water are heard, so sound travels through solids and liquids.
The material through which sound propagates is a medium; a space with no matter is a vacuum.

subsections.title: Sound needs a medium to propagate
points: In the vacuum bell jar experiment the bell's sound fades as air is pumped out, though the bell is seen ringing.
Sound cannot propagate in vacuum; astronauts on spacewalks communicate through devices in their suits.

sections.title: Sound Waves
points: A pushed slinky shows regions of close and spread-out turns travelling along it while each turn only oscillates.
An oscillating piston in an air-filled tube creates compressions (higher density) and rarefactions (lower density) that travel away.
A sound wave is a series of alternating compressions and rarefactions propagating without actual flow of particles; a point source gives spherical waves.
In longitudinal waves particles vibrate parallel to propagation; in transverse waves perpendicular. Waves needing a medium are mechanical waves.
Firecrackers and thunder create sudden density disturbances; a supersonic aircraft makes a sonic boom; light is a transverse wave that travels in vacuum.

sections.title: Energy of Sound Waves
points: A loud sound makes grains jump on a stretched sheet without touching it, showing sound carries energy.
Energy is transferred through vibrations and collisions of particles, not by the particles travelling.
A microphone converts sound energy to electrical signals through a vibrating diaphragm; a speaker does the opposite.

sections.title: Graphical Representation of a Sound Wave
points: At an instant, the density of the medium varies periodically with distance from the source.
A graph of density against distance shows variation above and below the average density.
The highest point (maximum density, compression) is the crest and the lowest point (minimum density, rarefaction) is the trough.

sections.title: Characteristics of a Sound Wave
points: Sound waves are described by wavelength, frequency, time period, amplitude, intensity and speed.

subsections.title: Wavelength, frequency and time period
points: Wavelength (λ) is the distance between consecutive crests or troughs, in metres.
Frequency (ν) is the number of density oscillations at a fixed point per unit time, in hertz (Hz).
Time period (T) is the time for one complete oscillation; ν = 1/T.
Musical notes Sa to Sa have increasing frequencies; 10 oscillations in 2 s give 5 Hz and T = 0.2 s.

subsections.title: Amplitude and intensity of the sound waves
points: Amplitude is the maximum change in density in a compression or rarefaction compared to average density.
A larger amplitude wave carries more energy.
Intensity is sound energy passing through unit area perpendicular to propagation per unit time; it decreases with distance as sound spreads.

subsections.title: Speed of Sound
points: Speed of sound is the distance a crest or trough travels in unit time: v = λ/T = νλ.
Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases (steel 5000, water 1500, air 340 m s–1 at 15 °C).
Speed in air rises with temperature and humidity: about 331 m s–1 at 0 °C and 344 m s–1 at 22 °C.
In most media speed depends only on the medium, not frequency; human hearing limits of 20 Hz and 20 kHz correspond to 17.2 m and 1.72 cm in air.
Lightning 5 s before thunder is about 1.7 km away.

subsections.title: Human perception of sound
points: Loudness and pitch are subjective perceptions without simple relations to physical properties.

subsections.title: Pitch
points: Pitch is how frequency is perceived; shrill sounds have high pitch and deep sounds low pitch.
The audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; below is infrasonic and above is ultrasonic. Dogs, bats and dolphins detect ultrasound; elephants detect infrasound.

subsections.title: Loudness
points: Loudness is how amplitude is perceived; larger amplitude sounds louder and loudness falls with distance.
Intensity is measurable while loudness depends on the listener; loudness is measured in decibels (conversation about 60 dB, firecrackers over 100 dB).
Noise is unwanted or harmful sound and can cause hearing loss.
Timbre is the unique quality of instruments from their overtones; an octave is an interval where one note has double the frequency; C. V. Raman studied the tabla and mridangam.

sections.title: Reflection of Sound
points: Sound bounces off obstacles and follows the same laws of reflection as light.

subsections.title: Echo
points: An echo is sound reflected from a distant hard surface and heard again.
Two sounds must be at least 0.1 s apart to be heard separately, so the minimum echo distance is 17 m (at 340 m s–1).
Hard smooth surfaces give strong echoes; soft surfaces absorb and rough surfaces scatter sound.
An echo after 0.5 s means the wall is 85 m away.

subsections.title: Reverberation
points: Multiple reflections making sound persist after the source stops are reverberation, when reflections arrive less than 0.05 s apart.
Auditoriums use absorbing panels, upholstered chairs and curtains to control reverberation; the Gol Gumbaz Whispering Gallery shows acoustic design.

sections.title: Ultrasonic and Infrasonic Waves, and their Applications
points: Infrasonic waves help detect earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and severe storms.
Ultrasonic waves are used in ultrasonography, breaking kidney stones, welding and cleaning, detecting defects in metal and locating objects.

subsections.title: Echolocation
points: Bats emit ultrasonic bursts and sense echoes to locate obstacles and prey; dolphins, whales and some birds also use echolocation.
Sonar sends ultrasonic waves into water to find distance, direction and speed of underwater objects; a 0.90 s echo at 1530 m s–1 means 688.5 m.
Audio surveillance detects drones and aircraft from their low-frequency humming.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Questions on sound as a mechanical wave, effect of frequency, and echo versus reverberation.
Reading and drawing density–distance graphs for wavelength, amplitude and frequency.
Numerical problems on time period, sonar depth, parking sensors, temperature effect on thunder delay, and speed ratio in air and water.
