bookSummary: Sound is produced by vibrating objects.
Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave that needs a medium to travel.
Sound can propagate through solids, liquids and gases.
In sound propagation, the density disturbance travels, not the particles of the medium, which only vibrate about their mean positions.
The distance between two consecutive crests or troughs is the wavelength.
The change in density at a fixed point from maximum to minimum and back to maximum (or vice versa) makes one complete oscillation.
The number of density oscillations at a fixed point per unit time is the frequency.
The time taken for one complete density oscillation at a fixed point is the time period.
The amplitude is the maximum change in air density in a compression or rarefaction compared to the average density.
The intensity of sound is the sound energy passing through a unit area perpendicular to propagation in unit time.
The speed of sound is the distance a point on a wave, such as a crest or trough, travels in unit time.
Echoes and reverberations are heard because of reflection of sound from various surfaces.
Sound waves below 20 Hz are infrasonic waves; above 20 kHz are ultrasonic waves.

chapters.title: Reproduction: How Life Continues
chapters.overview: The chapter explains reproduction as the process by which organisms produce new individuals of their kind. It covers asexual reproduction (vegetative propagation and its agricultural methods, budding, spore formation) and sexual reproduction, showing how meiosis creates variation. It describes flowers, pollination strategies, fertilisation and seed formation in plants, fertilisation strategies in animals, and human reproduction including the reproductive systems, gametogenesis, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, maternal health, sexual maturity, STIs and contraception.

sections.title: Asexual Reproduction
points: Asexual reproduction occurs in bacteria, amoeba, yeast, hydra, sponges and many plants.
Potato, ginger, money plant and sugarcane cuttings, and Bryophyllum leaves, produce new plants by vegetative propagation from vegetative parts.
It involves one parent and produces genetically identical individuals.
Yeast in sugar solution shows buds emerging; in hydra a bud forms by repeated cell division, grows and separates (budding).
Louis Pasteur showed life comes from pre-existing life, founded the germ theory of disease and led to sterilisation.
Bread mould grows from airborne spores; spores form in sacs (Rhizopus) or on vesicles of hyphae (Aspergillus), are light and produced in millions.
Asexual reproduction is based on mitosis, so offspring are clones; it increases population fast in favourable conditions.
Refrigeration slows moulds; fungi degrade wastes and give antibiotics like penicillin.

subsections.title: How is vegetative propagation in plants helpful in agriculture?
points: Cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture let farmers grow desirable crops on a large scale.
Tissue culture from shoot tips gives virus-free banana plantlets; KVKs train farmers in grafting.

subsections.title: Cutting
points: Overgrown branches are cut at the end of the growing season; cuttings with lower leaves removed are inserted half their length in soil with compost at about 45–60° and watered.

subsections.title: Grafting
points: A stem piece from Plant B (e.g. yellow or pink rose) is fitted into a slit on a healthy rooted Plant A (wild rose), wrapped to keep out pests, and other branches of A are cut.

subsections.title: Layering
points: The middle of a flexible twig (e.g. lemon) is buried in soil; roots develop in 10–15 days and the twig is then cut from the parent to grow as a new plant.

sections.title: Sexual Reproduction
points: Sexual reproduction involves two parents contributing genetic material.
Meiosis prevents the chromosome number doubling each generation.

subsections.title: How does meiosis help create variations in sexual reproduction?
points: Humans have 23 pairs (46) of chromosomes; meiosis reduces diploid cells to haploid gametes with 23.
Male gametes are sperm and female gametes eggs; in plants pollen carries male gametes to the ovule.
A bead model shows three pairs of characters give eight combinations; 23 pairs give very many.
Random mixing makes children different from parents and siblings; variation aids adaptation and evolution.

subsections.title: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
points: Flowers are reproductive organs of angiosperms; a complete flower has sepals, petals, stamens and pistil.
The stamen (filament and anther) produces pollen with male gametes; the pistil has stigma, style and ovary with ovules containing eggs.
In a pea plant experiment, fruit did not form only where stamens were removed from a bagged bud, showing pollen transfer is needed.
Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma is pollination.

subsections.title: How does the process of pollination occur in flowers?
points: Self-pollination is transfer to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant.
Cross-pollination is transfer to a flower of another plant of the same type.

subsections.title: Pollination strategies and reproductive success
points: Pollinators include wind, water, insects and birds.
Wind-pollinated wheat, maize and rice have light, numerous pollen and feathery stigmas; Vallisneria and Hydrilla use water.
Insect-pollinated sunflower, hibiscus and marigold have bright, fragrant, nectar-rich flowers with sticky pollen; coral tree and hibiscus are also bird-pollinated.

subsections.title: Fertilisation and seed formation
points: Pollen tubes grow through the style to the ovule, where the male gamete fuses with the egg (fertilisation), forming a zygote that becomes an embryo.
The ovary becomes the fruit and ovules become seeds, dispersed by wind, water or animals.
Wind-pollinated grasses release far more pollen but form fewer seeds than insect-pollinated plants.
Plant breeding uses selective breeding, artificial hybridisation and genetic engineering; P. Maheshwari pioneered in-vitro fertilisation in flowering plants.

sections.title: Sexual Reproduction in Animals
points: In frogs and most fish, eggs and sperm are released into water: external fertilisation, with many eggs lost.
In reptiles, birds and mammals fertilisation occurs inside the female: internal fertilisation, giving better protection and survival.

sections.title: Variations in Reproduction in Animals
points: Fish and frogs lay hundreds to thousands of eggs with low survival; lizards and birds lay few eggs with moderate to high survival.
Many-egg species have little yolk per egg; a feeding larva hatches and later transforms into an adult, as in butterflies and frogs.
Reptile and bird eggs carry enough yolk until hatching; in mammals the zygote develops inside the female and young are fed milk.

sections.title: Reproduction in Human Beings
points: The human reproductive system forms gametes, which meet to form a zygote that develops into an embryo and foetus in the uterus.

subsections.title: Reproductive maturity
points: As children grow into adults, reproductive organs mature and begin producing sperm or eggs.

subsections.title: What are the parts of the male reproductive system?
points: Testes in the scrotum produce sperm and a hormone controlling sperm production and puberty changes; the scrotum keeps them cooler.
Sperm travel through the vas deferens to the urethra; seminal vesicles and prostate add nourishing fluids.
Each sperm has a head with genetic material and a tail for swimming.

subsections.title: What are the parts of the female reproductive system?
points: The female system has two ovaries, oviducts (fallopian tubes), uterus and vagina.
Ovaries produce eggs and hormones; the uterus is where the foetus develops and opens into the vagina through the cervix.

subsections.title: How are reproductive cells made?
points: Gametogenesis in testes and ovaries forms gametes by meiosis: 46 chromosomes become 23.
Males produce millions of tiny motile sperm without stored nutrients; females produce a single large non-motile egg with nutrients.

subsections.title: What happens when a sperm meets an egg?
points: From puberty usually one mature egg is released each month (ovulation) and the uterine lining thickens.
A sperm fusing with the egg in the oviduct forms a zygote, which divides and implants in the uterine lining, beginning pregnancy.
IVF combines egg and sperm outside the body; Subhash Mukhopadhyay pioneered India's first test tube baby in 1978.

subsections.title: What happens when an egg is not fertilised?
points: An unfertilised egg degenerates in about a day and the uterine lining sheds with blood: menstruation, lasting 3 to 7 days.
The cycle repeats every 21–35 days (often 28), from about age 10–14 to menopause around 50; ovulation is around day 14.
Females have XX and males XY; the father's X or Y determines the baby's sex.
Menstrual hygiene includes using clean products, washing hands, changing pads every 4–6 hours and proper disposal.

subsections.title: Pregnancy and childbirth
points: Pregnancy lasts about nine months in three trimesters; from about the ninth week the embryo is called a foetus.
Uterine muscle contractions push the baby out; medical or surgical procedures help when needed.
Newborns need breastfeeding, warmth and vaccination; mothers need nutrition, rest and to avoid smoking, alcohol and unprescribed medicines.

subsections.title: Mother’s health during pregnancy
points: A balanced diet, regular check-ups, suitable exercise and rest, and emotional support keep mother and baby healthy.
ASHA workers promote maternal care; post-partum depression is a treatable condition.

subsections.title: What does it mean to be sexually mature?
points: Sexual maturation makes the body capable of reproduction but does not mean readiness for adult responsibilities.
Emotional maturity — handling feelings, communicating and making thoughtful decisions — takes longer.

subsections.title: How can unwanted pregnancies and infections be prevented?
points: Responsible choices help prevent unplanned pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts, HIV).
Contraceptives include barriers like condoms, hormonal oral pills, IUDs like copper-T and surgical blocking of vas deferens or fallopian tubes.
Prenatal sex determination is prohibited by law in India to protect the sex ratio; CDRI Lucknow developed a non-steroidal weekly contraceptive pill.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Questions on pollination type, ordering stages of plant reproduction and an assertion on implantation.
Reasoning on clones, menstrual cycle in pregnancy, night-blooming flowers, self-pollination and disease risk.
Experimental design with pollen germination, pollination in tomato, wheat and papaya, and apple yields with beekeeping.

keyTerms.meaning: A biological process by which living beings produce new individuals of their own kind.
Reproduction by a single parent producing offspring that are almost exact copies of it.

Methods of vegetative propagation using shoot pieces, joining a stem piece into a rooted plant, and rooting a buried twig.

Green outer whorl protecting the bud, and coloured projections of a flower.
Male part of a flower: filament and anther producing pollen.
Female part of a flower: stigma, style and ovary.
The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower.
Pollen transfer within the same flower or plant, and to a flower of another plant of the same type.

Fusion of male and female gametes.
The fertilised egg, which develops into an embryo.
Fertilisation outside the body in water, and inside the female's body.
Intermediate feeding stage hatching from an egg before transformation into an adult.

Infections transmitted through sexual contact, e.g. gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts, HIV.
A pregnancy-preventing method such as condoms, pills or IUDs.

keyResults.label: Human chromosome number
keyResults.statement: Body cells have 23 pairs (46) chromosomes; sperm and eggs have 23.

keyResults.label: Bead model
keyResults.statement: Three pairs of characters give eight possible combinations in gametes.

keyResults.label: Plant fertilisation outcome
keyResults.statement: After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

keyResults.label: Pollen and seed data
keyResults.statement: Wind-pollinated grasses: 5,00,000–10,00,000 pollen grains per flower, 50–200 seeds; insect-pollinated sunflower: 20,000–40,000 pollen, 800–1,000 seeds.

keyResults.label: Menstrual cycle
keyResults.statement: Repeats every 21–35 days (often 28); menstruation days 1–5, ovulation about day 14; begins at 10–14 years and continues to menopause around 50.

keyResults.label: Sex determination
keyResults.statement: Mother contributes X; father contributes X (female, XX) or Y (male, XY).

keyResults.label: Pregnancy
keyResults.statement: Lasts about nine months in three trimesters; embryo called foetus from about the ninth week.

keyResults.label: Date: 1978
keyResults.statement: Subhash Mukhopadhyay of Kolkata pioneered India's first test tube baby.

bookSummary: Reproduction is the biological process by which living organisms produce new individuals of the same species, ensuring continuity of life and transfer of genetic information.
There are two main types of reproduction: asexual and sexual.
Asexual reproduction occurs in different ways, such as budding, spore formation and vegetative propagation in plants.
A flower is the reproductive organ of a plant, with male stamen and female pistil.
Pollination is the process of pollen transfer from anther to stigma, through self- or cross-pollination.
During fertilisation, the pollen tube carries the sperm cells to the ovule, where they fuse to form a zygote; the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit.
In humans, the testes produce sperm; glands like testes, seminal vesicles and prostate produce male hormones.
Ovaries produce eggs and female hormones; ovulation takes place around the 14th day of the menstrual cycle.
Birth control methods include condoms, pills, IUDs (Copper-T), etc.
If fertilisation occurs, the zygote develops into an embryo and pregnancy begins, usually lasting about nine months.
The mother needs proper nutrition, check-ups and rest, and should avoid harmful substances during pregnancy.

chapters.title: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
chapters.overview: The chapter introduces biodiversity, India's biodiversity hotspots and endemic species, and how diversity evolved. It explains criteria for classifying organisms, the need for classification and the history of classification systems leading to Whittaker's five kingdoms. It describes Monera, Protista, Fungi, the five classes of Plantae and the phyla of Animalia through vertebrates, then covers adaptations, the hierarchy of classification, binomial nomenclature, the three domain system, fossils and threats to biodiversity.

sections.title: India as a Biodiversity Hotspot
points: Biodiversity is the immense variety of living organisms; every organism helps keep nature stable, and farmers conserved diverse crop varieties.
India's mountains, deserts, rainforests, plateaus and coasts have different soils and climates supporting many species.
Endemic species are restricted to particular regions, e.g. Nilgiri tahr, Lion-tailed macaque, Nepenthes khasiana and Neelakurinji.
Biodiversity hotspots have many endemic species and significant habitat loss, e.g. Western Ghats, Indo-Burma, Himalayas and Sundaland.

sections.title: How has the Biodiversity Evolved?
points: Small differences among individuals affected survival and reproduction and accumulated over generations into new forms of life.
Today's diversity results from continuous change over vast time, and classification provides a framework to study it.
Sangam Tinai classification of landscapes and sacred groves preserved diverse habitats.

sections.title: How to Classify Organisms?
points: Animals in an ecosystem picture can be grouped by where they live, when they are active or what they eat.
The same organism fits different groups depending on the criterion chosen, leading to the idea of classification.

subsections.title: Some criteria to classify living organisms
points: Criteria include external features, mode of nutrition, internal structures and cell structure.
Ecological role, reproduction and genetic similarity studied using DNA are also used.
Similar features suggest evolution from common ancestors.

sections.title: The Need for Classification
points: Like arranging books in a library, classifying millions of organisms helps us understand them.
Pakke Tiger Reserve has nearly 300 of India's about 1,300 bird species and four hornbill species that depend on large old trees.
Biological classification is the scientific system of grouping organisms by similarities and differences.
It organises study, shows relationships, helps name new organisms, supports conservation and gives scientists a common system.

sections.title: Biological Classification Systems Over Time
points: Aristotle (4th century BCE) grouped animals by habitat and external appearance.
The two kingdom system (Linnaeus, 1758) divided life into Plantae and Animalia, but could not place Amoeba, Paramecium or bacteria.
Protista was added for unicellular microscopic organisms (Haeckel, 1866); bacteria without a true nucleus were placed in Monera (Copeland, 1938).
Fungi, heterotrophs absorbing nutrients, were separated, giving Whittaker's five kingdoms (1969); the Rigveda and Brihat Samhita classified animals by habitat and behaviour.

sections.title: Five Kingdom Classification
points: The five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Criteria are cell type (prokaryote or eukaryote), cell structure (cell wall), level of organisation (unicellular or multicellular) and mode of nutrition.

subsections.title: Kingdom Monera — Unicellular prokaryotes
points: Bacteria and cyanobacteria are single-celled prokaryotes found everywhere, including extreme environments and inside bodies.
Some bacteria are pathogens but many are useful (Lactobacillus, Rhizobium); gut bacteria of ruminants produce biogas and some break down pollutants.
Cyanobacteria were among the first oxygen producers; their fossils (stromatolites) are found in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.
Ram Bux Singh set up India's first scientifically designed biogas plant in 1957.

subsections.title: Kingdom Protista — Unicellular eukaryotes
points: Single-celled eukaryotes without a cell wall or with a cellulose wall, e.g. Amoeba, Euglena, Paramecium, seen in hay infusion.
They live in water or moist places; some are autotrophic and some heterotrophic.
They link aquatic food chains, produce oxygen, feed small animals and some decompose matter.

subsections.title: Kingdom Fungi — Multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes with a cell wall
points: Fungi are mostly multicellular with chitin cell walls and absorb nutrients through filaments forming mycelium.
Most are saprophytes and decomposers; some are symbiotic and some parasitic; they reproduce often by spores.
Yeast is unicellular but placed in fungi due to its chitin wall; Aspergillus and Penicillium give enzymes and antibiotics.
Wild edible mushrooms are known to tribal communities and mushroom farming is a livelihood.

subsections.title: Kingdom Plantae — Multicellular, autotrophic eukaryotes with a cell wall
points: Plants photosynthesise, have cellulose cell walls, form the base of food chains and release oxygen.
Plantae is divided into five classes: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperm and Angiosperm.
From algae to angiosperms, plants evolved transport tissues, seeds and flowers to meet the challenges of life on land.

subsections.title: Thallophyta (algae) — Primitive plants
points: Simplest plants in water or moist places, with a thallus body that exchanges gases, nutrients and water directly, e.g. Spirogyra.
Lichens, symbiotic algae and fungi, are bioindicators of air quality and used as spice, medicine and dyes.

subsections.title: Bryophyta — First steps on land, still need water
points: Mosses and liverworts (Marchantia) grow as green mats in moist, shady places and have rhizoids and simple stem- and leaf-like parts.
They need water for reproduction and are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.

subsections.title: Pteridophyta — Adaptation to land and having structural transport system
points: Ferns have true roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissues, xylem and phloem.
They still need water for reproduction and do not produce seeds.

subsections.title: Gymnosperms — Reproduction without water
points: Pines and cycads suit cold, dry regions, with needle-like or scale-like leaves that reduce water loss.
They produce naked seeds, often exposed on cones, and do not need water for fertilisation.

subsections.title: Angiosperms — Efficient reproduction and seed dispersal
points: Flowering plants have the most complex body organisation and produce flowers and fruits.
Flowers attract pollinators and fruits spread seeds, making angiosperms the most diverse plant group; leaves can be grouped as monocots or dicots.
Hortus Malabaricus, compiled by van Rheede with Itty Achudan in the 17th century, described Indian plants and medicinal uses.

subsections.title: Kingdom Animalia — Multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes
points: Animals depend on others for food and show locomotion, rapid response and coordinated behaviour.
Presence or absence of a notochord, a flexible rod, divides animals into non-chordata (invertebrata) and chordata.
Chordata is further divided into protochordata and vertebrata.

subsections.title: Invertebrates — Animals without a notochord
points: Invertebrates lack a notochord but range from simple bodies to complex organ systems, showing how the animal body changed over time.

subsections.title: Porifera (pore-bearers) — Multicellularity without tissues
points: Sponges are fixed, aquatic and multicellular without tissues; water flowing through pores brings food and oxygen; a kilogram of sponge can filter up to 24,000 litres a day.

subsections.title: Cnidaria — True tissues and active feeding
points: Hydra, jellyfish and corals have tissue-level organisation and capture prey with tentacles but have a single opening for food intake and waste.

subsections.title: Platyhelminthes (flatworms) — Bilateral symmetry and directional movement
points: Flatworms have bilateral symmetry and flattened bodies for diffusion, a single opening, and parasitic forms with hooks and suckers; hygiene prevents worm infections.

subsections.title: Nematoda (roundworms) — Efficient body design with two openings
points: Roundworms have elongated cylindrical bodies with mouth and anus and organ system level organisation, and live in soil, water or hosts.

subsections.title: Annelida (segmented worms) — segmentation and body cavities
points: Earthworms have cylindrical segmented bodies with muscles, a nerve cord and a body cavity, giving flexible, controlled movement.

subsections.title: Arthropoda — Jointed appendages and an external skeleton
points: Insects, crabs and spiders have segmented bodies with specialised segments and a hard external skeleton that protects, reduces water loss and supports muscles.

subsections.title: Mollusca — Organ system level organisation with soft bodies
points: Snails, squids and octopuses have soft bodies, often protected by a shell, with a distinct head, muscular foot and hump.

subsections.title: Echinodermata — Internal support without a notochord
points: Starfish and sea urchins have a hard internal skeleton of calcium carbonate that gives protection and controlled movement.

subsections.title: Looking across invertebrates
points: From sponges to echinoderms, body organisation increases in complexity, improving feeding, movement and protection while introducing new challenges.

subsections.title: Protochordates — The appearance of the notochord
points: Protochordates like Amphioxus have a notochord at least once in life, giving internal support; they show how chordates may have arisen.

subsections.title: Vertebrates — Animals with a backbone
points: Vertebrates have a vertebral column protecting the brain and spinal cord, allowing larger size and complex organ systems.
They are grouped as fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Diverse forests reduce disaster impacts: mangroves limited the 1999 Orissa super cyclone damage and forest diversity limits Kyasanur Forest Disease.

sections.title: Adaptations as Outcomes of Structural Change
points: Fins and gills suit fish to water; feathers and hollow bones make bird flight possible.
Fat storage in camels and thick fur in polar bears support survival in extreme conditions; mammary glands improve survival of young mammals.

subsections.title: The hierarchical nature of classification
points: Classification goes from broad to specific: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
At lower levels organisms share more features, and each group is part of the one above, like an address.
Tiger: Animalia, Chordata, Vertebrata, Mammalia, Carnivora, Felidae, Panthera, P. tigris; pea: Plantae, Magnoliophyta, Magnoliopsida, Fabales, Fabaceae, Pisum, P. sativum.

sections.title: Scientific Naming — The Binomial System
points: Common names differ by language, so Carolus Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature in the 18th century.
Each scientific name has a genus and species part in Latin, e.g. Panthera tigris, Mangifera indica.
A genus groups closely related species (Panthera tigris and Panthera leo); a species is similar individuals able to interbreed.
Carl Woese (1977) proposed the three domain system — Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya — based on genetic data.

subsections.title: Rules for writing the scientific names
points: The name has two parts, genus and species.
The genus begins with a capital letter and comes first; the species is in lower case.
The name is italicised when printed or underlined when handwritten.

sections.title: Fossils as Evidence
points: Fossils are preserved remains of plants and animals in layers of rock, sand and mud.
Older layers generally hold simpler organisms and newer layers more complex forms, recording how life changed.
Birbal Sahni studied fossil plants and founded BSIP in Lucknow; classification systems change as science learns more.

sections.title: Biodiversity Under Threat
points: Every species has a role: plants make food and oxygen, animals pollinate and disperse seeds, microbes recycle nutrients.
Pollution, deforestation, overuse of resources and climate change reduce biodiversity, and loss of one species affects others.
The Purple Frog (Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis), discovered in 2003, is named after the Sahyadri Hills.
The endangered Sangai deer of Manipur's phumdis in Loktak lake was declared extinct in 1951 and rediscovered in 1953.

sections.title: Revise, Reflect, Refine
points: Identifying insects versus earthworms and the animal features of sponges.
Reasoning on classification criteria, protists with cilia, viruses and the limits of the five kingdom system.
A case study classifying organisms P to T from structural, cellular and nutritional observations.

keyTerms.meaning: The immense variety of living organisms on the Earth.
Species restricted to particular regions and not found naturally anywhere else.
Regions with a large number of endemic species that have undergone significant habitat loss.
The scientific system of grouping living organisms based on similarities and differences.
Kingdom of unicellular prokaryotes such as bacteria and cyanobacteria.
Kingdom of single-celled eukaryotes without a cell wall or with a cellulose wall.
Kingdom of mostly multicellular heterotrophic eukaryotes with chitin cell walls.
Network of fine fungal filaments through which nutrients are absorbed.
Organisms that feed on dead organic matter; most fungi.
Kingdom of multicellular autotrophic eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls.
Simple undifferentiated plant body of thallophytes.
Symbiotic associations of an autotrophic alga and a heterotrophic fungus; bioindicators of air quality.
Root-like structures of bryophytes.
Plants with naked seeds not enclosed in fruits (gymnos: naked, spermos: seed).
Flowering plants with seeds enclosed in fruits (angeion: vessel).
Kingdom of multicellular heterotrophic eukaryotes.

bookSummary: Life on the Earth exists in many forms, from simple bacteria to complex animals.
Scientists classify organisms based on cell structure, number of cells, mode of nutrition and ecological role.
Whittaker’s five kingdom classification — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia — is a simple and useful system to understand diversity.
Kingdom Plantae is divided into five classes — Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperm and Angiosperm.

Kingdom Animalia is divided into non-chordata (invertebrates) and chordata on the basis of the notochord; non-chordata is divided into Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata.
Protochordates show a transition from invertebrates to vertebrates as they possess a notochord at least once in their life; vertebrates are divided into fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Classification helps us understand relationships among organisms, trace the history of life on the Earth and conserve biodiversity.

chapters.title: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
chapters.overview: The chapter treats the Earth as one system of interacting spheres — geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere and biosphere — through which energy and matter flow. It explains uneven heating by solar radiation (electromagnetic spectrum, insolation, solar constant, albedo, latitude and the layered atmosphere) and how it drives local winds, planetary winds and ocean currents. It describes the water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles and how human activities disrupt them, and ends with ways to restore balance.

sections.title: Activity 13.1: Let us explore
points: Life is powered by a flow of energy and matter; the Sun is the main energy source, along with the Earth's hot interior and chemical reactions.
The Earth system has five spheres: geosphere (rocks, soil, interior), hydrosphere (liquid water), cryosphere (ice and snow), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (living organisms and habitats).
A disturbance in one sphere changes others: less snowfall lowers lake levels and grass for sheep.
Warmer Arabian Sea water increases evaporation and makes the southwest monsoon variable, while melting ice may raise sea levels and cause habitat loss.

sections.title: Uneven Heating of the Earth
points: Solar radiation reaches the Earth as electromagnetic waves travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m s–1 through vacuum.
The electromagnetic spectrum ranges from high-frequency gamma rays and X-rays to low-frequency infrared and radio waves; about 99% of solar energy is UV, visible and IR.
The ozone layer absorbs UV; visible light drives photosynthesis; IR warms the surface, and greenhouse gases trap part of the re-radiated heat.
Insolation is the Sun's radiation reaching the surface; the solar constant is about 1.4 kW m–2 at the top of the atmosphere, and surface insolation is about 1 kW m–2 under clear skies.
Anna Mani mapped solar insolation over India; 1 kW m–2 on 1 m² for an hour gives 3.6 × 10⁶ J, one unit of electricity.

subsections.title: Interaction of solar radiation on the Earth’s surface
points: Land heats faster than water; dark surfaces absorb more sunlight and light surfaces reflect more.
Albedo is the fraction of solar radiation reflected; snow (0.80–0.90) and ice have high albedo, black soil and ocean water low.
Concrete houses re-radiate heat at night while mud houses stay cool.
The urban heat island effect makes cities warmer than rural areas because built materials absorb and retain heat.

subsections.title: Latitude and Earth’s shape
points: On a spherical Earth, sunlight is concentrated over a small area at the equator and spread over a large area near the poles.
Equatorial regions stay warm and polar regions cold; the tilt of the axis causes seasons.
This uneven heating drives global winds and ocean currents.

subsections.title: Role of the atmosphere
points: The atmosphere, held by gravity, is mainly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%).
Weather occurs in the troposphere (0–12 km) where temperature falls about 6.5 °C/km; in the stratosphere (12–50 km) ozone absorbs UV and temperature rises with height.
Outer space begins at about 100 km; the atmosphere absorbs incoming radiation and traps outgoing heat, but excess CO2 causes global warming (Venus is hotter than Mercury).
CFCs caused the ozone hole over Antarctica; the Montreal Protocol is allowing recovery; K. R. Ramanathan measured Himalayan ozone in 1934.

sections.title: Uneven Heating Causes Wind and Ocean Currents
points: Wind moves from high to low pressure; pressure differences come mainly from uneven heating, as in land and sea breezes.

subsections.title: Local winds
points: By day, sunlit slopes heat faster, warm air rises and cooler valley air moves up: a valley breeze.
After sunset, slopes cool faster and cold dense air flows down into the valley: a mountain breeze, common in Shimla and Dehradun.

subsections.title: Planetary winds
points: Rising air at the equator forms the equatorial low pressure belt; air sinking near 30° N and S forms sub-tropical high pressure belts.
Air rising near 60° forms sub-polar low pressure belts; cold sinking air at the poles forms polar high pressure belts.
The Earth's rotation deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere.

subsections.title: Ocean currents
points: Ocean currents are continuous movements of large water masses driven by winds, temperature and salinity differences, rotation and land masses.
Warm equatorial water flows poleward at the surface and cold dense water returns at depth; rotation forms gyres, clockwise in the north.
Currents move heat poleward; the North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, keeps northwest European ports ice-free.
IITM Pune runs coupled models of atmosphere, ocean, land and ice to forecast the monsoon.

sections.title: Biogeochemical Cycles
points: Living organisms constantly exchange matter and energy with air, water, soil and rocks.
The cyclic movement of matter and energy between abiotic and biotic components is a biogeochemical cycle, recycling carbon, nitrogen and oxygen.

subsections.title: Water cycle
points: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation and flows back to the ocean, with some seeping underground and dissolving minerals.
Climate change causes heavier rain in some places and drought in others; melting glaciers raise sea levels threatening Mumbai and Chennai.
Intense rainfall increases runoff and erosion and reduces groundwater recharge, linking all spheres.

subsections.title: Carbon cycle
points: Carbon in all biomolecules moves between atmosphere, biosphere, geosphere and hydrosphere.
In the fast cycle (days to years) photosynthesis takes in CO2 and respiration and decomposition return it.
In the slow cycle (millions of years) buried organisms become fossil fuels, whose burning quickly releases CO2; oceans absorb CO2 as carbonate and bicarbonate used by phytoplankton and shells.

Atmospheric CO2 rose about 35% since 1960 (315 to 420 ppm, the Keeling curve), intensifying the greenhouse effect; carbon is about 49% of dry weight of organisms and 71% of global carbon is in oceans.

subsections.title: Nitrogen cycle
points: Nitrogen, needed for proteins and nucleic acids, is abundant in air as unreactive N2 that must be converted before use.
Nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium and Azotobacter makes ammonia; nitrification by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter gives nitrite then nitrate.
Plants assimilate nitrates; decomposers return ammonia (ammonification); Pseudomonas returns nitrogen gas (denitrification); lightning also fixes nitrogen.
The Haber-Bosch process (early 1900s) makes most fertiliser ammonia, enabling the Green Revolution but using 1–2% of global energy.

subsections.title: Oxygen cycle
points: About 21% of the atmosphere is O2; oxygen is also in biomolecules, crustal oxides and CO2.
Respiration and combustion use oxygen and release CO2; photosynthesis restores oxygen, balancing it across the spheres.

sections.title: Human Impact on Earth’s Processes
points: Excess CO2 makes seawater more acidic, threatening plankton and coral reefs, while warmer water absorbs less CO2.
Fossil fuel burning and deforestation saturate carbon sinks; fertiliser nitrates cause algal blooms that deplete oxygen (eutrophication).
Deforestation reduces photosynthesis, transpiration and rainfall, alters albedo, increases erosion and destroys habitats; vehicle emissions form smog and ground-level ozone.
The Montreal Protocol is repairing the ozone layer, while the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement have been less successful.
Conserving energy, renewable energy, tree planting, saving water, sustainable farming and Mission LiFE (2021) help restore balance.

points: Multiple-choice questions on the role of biogeochemical cycles and warming of the Earth.

bookSummary: The electromagnetic radiation received from the Sun is the primary source of energy on the Earth.
Most weather processes like evaporation, condensation and precipitation occur in the troposphere.
The shape of the Earth, latitude and tilt of the Earth’s axis are primarily responsible for variations in insolation, and hence, for uneven heating of the Earth’s surface.
Uneven heating of the Earth’s surface is responsible for the generation of winds and ocean currents.
Matter and energy are continuously cycled between the living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) systems.
Atmospheric oxygen is used in combustion, respiration and oxide formation, and is restored mainly through photosynthesis.
Water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen continuously cycle between the atmosphere, oceans, land and living organisms.
Biogeochemical cycles make nutrients available to living organisms, sustain life, regulate climate and balance ecosystems.
